before: Archai is not a “crypto project.” It is institutional infrastructure. So it must obey institutional physics.

before: A “token” is not a secured asset unless it maps to enforceable rights. Archai vault assets are always paired with a real legal wrapper (SPV, trust, foundation, coop) that holds title and signs a protocol-aligned charter. This must be made explicit and primary.
after: A token requires enforceable rights to represent a secured asset. Archai vault assets are always paired with a real legal wrapper (SPV, trust, foundation, coop) that holds title and signs a protocol-aligned charter. The design must make these enforceable rights explicit from the outset.

before: We treat built assets as cash-flow machines (housing, services, utilities, data, commerce). Appreciation is not the core promise.
after: We treat built assets as sources of cash flow (housing, services, utilities, data, commerce). Appreciation is not the core promise.

before: Mass provides primitives (entities/ownership/identity/consent/etc.). Archai composes them into “built asset institutions.” This is exactly how Momentum describes the ecosystem architecture: Archai is the tokenization layer for HomeOS buildings that integrate natively with Mass primitives.
after: Mass provides primitives for entities, ownership, identity, consent, and related functions. Archai composes them into institutions that own and operate built assets. In Momentum’s architecture, Archai tokenizes HomeOS buildings through native integration with these primitives.

before: A system this complex needs an evidence layer. SEZ Legal Stack implements: Smart should generate cryptographically secured, legally enforceable attestation streams so compliance can be verified programmatically without exposing private data.
after: The system needs evidence for compliance checks. Under the SEZ Legal Stack design, Smart Assets should generate cryptographically secured, legally enforceable attestation streams. These let programs verify compliance without exposing private data.
